You don’t need to discover one perfect passion before you can make progress. Many people choose a direction by noticing what they enjoy doing, what they’re good at, and what kinds of working conditions suit them—and those preferences can change.

Start by paying attention to ordinary clues: Do you like solving problems, helping people, making things, explaining ideas, or organizing? Do you prefer working with others or independently, indoors or outdoors, with predictable routines or variety? Try different classes, clubs, volunteer work, part-time jobs, or short projects. You’re not committing to a career; you’re gathering evidence about what fits and what doesn’t.

You can also ask adults about what their jobs involve day to day, including the less appealing parts. A school counselor can help you explore options and plan classes without locking you in. For now, focus on building useful skills—communication, math, writing, teamwork, and curiosity—and keep a note of experiences you’d like to do more or less of.

A good place to start is by learning what children and teens in your area actually need. Contact local foster-care or child-welfare agencies, youth shelters, or organizations supporting young people who are homeless, and ask about volunteer roles, training, and screening requirements. Helping can mean many things besides becoming a foster parent: tutoring, mentoring, providing meals, supporting families in crisis, or helping young people find services.

Listen to young people without judging them, respect their privacy, and follow safeguarding rules. Advocacy also includes learning about housing and foster-care policies, sharing accurate information, and speaking up for stable, safe placements. If you’re considering fostering or adopting, ask an agency about the process and the specific needs involved. Start with one reliable organization and a role you can sustain.

The exact process depends on where you live, since licensing rules vary by state or country. In the U.S., start by checking your state cosmetology board’s website and looking up the requirements for a hairstylist, cosmetologist, or barber license. These titles can cover different services, and some places offer a narrower hair-only license.

Usually, you’ll need to be at least a certain age, complete an approved training program at a cosmetology school, and pass written and practical exams. Training hours vary considerably by location. Once you know the rules, contact a few approved schools to compare tuition, schedules, financial aid, and whether they help students prepare for licensing exams. Avoid enrolling until you’ve confirmed the program is recognized by your licensing board.

After completing the required training, apply to take the exams and submit any required fees or documents. Some areas also require a background check. Once you pass and receive your license, check renewal and continuing-education requirements before you begin working. If you share your state or country, someone can point you toward the specific steps.

“Engineering” covers many fields, so start by noticing what you enjoy: designing machines, building structures, working with electronics, writing code, improving manufacturing, or solving environmental problems. Take math and physics seriously, and try a hands-on project, robotics club, CAD course, coding activity, or summer program to see what suits you.

When comparing colleges, look for programs accredited by ABET in the United States, especially in the discipline you’re considering. Compare total cost, financial aid, graduation rates, internship and co-op options, and access to labs—not just rankings. Strong programs exist at many public universities and smaller schools; your state’s universities can be an excellent value.

Pay varies by specialty, location, experience, and industry. Software, electrical, chemical, and petroleum engineering can pay well, but salaries and job prospects change, and fit matters too. Explore job postings and salary data for roles that interest you. With good grades, ask a school counselor about prerequisites, scholarships, and application plans, and talk with practicing engineers or college students before choosing a path.
